content: Nitric oxide (NO) is a critical endogenous molecule that regulates vascular tone. Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) has been studied as a therapeutic intervention for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), a condition that can lead to severe hypoxemia in term and near-term infants. The primary objective of this research was to evaluate whether iNO improves oxygenation, reduces mortality, decreases the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and impacts long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes in hypoxemic term and near-term newborns. A comprehensive search was conducted using databases such as CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies up to January 2016. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials were included if they assessed clinically relevant outcomes, such as death, ECMO use, and oxygenation. Methodological quality was assessed using Cochrane Neonatal Review Group criteria, and statistical analyses were performed using risk ratios, risk differences, and weighted mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Seventeen eligible RCTs were identified, involving term and near-term infants with hypoxic respiratory failure. Ten trials compared iNO to a control group (placebo or standard care without iNO) in infants with moderate or severe illness. One trial allowed back-up iNO treatment for infants who remained severely ill after two hours. Another trial specifically studied infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Six trials compared immediate iNO treatment to delayed iNO treatment after clinical deterioration. The findings demonstrated that iNO improved outcomes in hypoxemic term and near-term infants by reducing the combined endpoint of death or ECMO use. This benefit was primarily due to a reduction in ECMO use, with a number needed to treat (NNT) of 5.3. However, iNO did not significantly reduce mortality. Approximately 50% of infants receiving iNO showed improved oxygenation. The oxygenation index (OI) decreased by a weighted mean of 15.1 within 30 to 60 minutes of therapy initiation, and the partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2) increased by an average of 53 mmHg. The response to iNO was not influenced by the presence of echocardiographic evidence of PPHN. However, infants with congenital diaphragmatic hernia did not experience improved outcomes with iNO; in fact, their outcomes were slightly worse, though not significantly so. Infants treated with iNO at less severe illness criteria did not show better clinical outcomes compared to those who received treatment only after their condition worsened. Early iNO treatment reduced disease progression but did not further decrease mortality or the need for ECMO. Long-term outcomes, including the incidence of disability, deafness, and developmental scores, were similar between survivors who received iNO and those who did not. In conclusion, inhaled nitric oxide, administered at an initial concentration of 20 ppm, is effective for term and near-term infants with hypoxic respiratory failure, provided they do not have a diaphragmatic hernia.
